Major-Minor Tonality. The system of organizing pitch and harmony that dominated Western music from roughly sixteen fifty to nineteen hundred and persists widely today. It anchors all music to a central note and uses two primary scales. The major scale is bright and stable. The minor scale is darker and more ambiguous. Together, they create harmonic and melodic unity. Understanding major-minor tonality is essential to grasping how classical, Baroque, and Romantic composers achieved both drama and coherence.

The major scale consists of a specific pattern of whole and half steps that produces a stable, affirmative sound. The minor scale exists in three forms: natural, harmonic, and melodic. Each alters the sixth and seventh scale degrees differently.

A key, such as C major or A minor, is the tonal center and set of pitches. The key signature indicates which notes are consistently sharp or flat. Every major key has a relative minor key sharing the same pitches but starting from a different note. C major and A minor share no accidentals.

Harmonic function, the role of chords as tension-builders or resolution points, depends entirely on their relationship to the tonal center. Modulation, changing keys mid-piece, creates drama and structural interest while remaining within the major-minor system.

The system collapsed in the early twentieth century when composers like Schoenberg and Debussy abandoned tonality for atonality and other systems. Tonality is the broader concept of which major-minor is the dominant historical implementation. Harmonic function is the system of chord roles, such as one, four, five, and so on, predicated on major-minor tonality. Chord progression sequences organize chords within major-minor tonal frameworks. Classical music is the era in which major-minor tonality reached its perfection and clarity. The key signature is the notational device indicating which major or minor key a piece uses. Modulation is the compositional technique of changing keys within a tonal piece.
